facts.raw_span: 1-week history of painful vision loss and floaters in her left eye
no history of myopia, ocular trauma, or surgery
Visual acuity was 20/30–2 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye
intraocular pressure was 21 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS
mild nuclear sclerotic cataract and no inflammation in the right eye
rare anterior chamber cells, 1+ vitreous cells, choroidal detachments in the nasal and temporal periphery, and an overlying retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid in the left eye
no retinal breaks were identified
Laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, HIV, T-spot, syphilis screen, and ANCA panel) were normal
MRI of the brain and orbits showed mild posterior scleral enhancement but no intraocular mass
Fluorescein angiography showed late leakage in the temporal periphery
fundus autofluorescence was normal
optical coherence tomography revealed shallow subretinal fluid and a posterior vitreous detachment

concepts.why: The patient presented with painful vision loss and floaters, and the MRI showed mild posterior scleral enhancement, which is consistent with posterior scleritis.
The patient had a retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid, and the fluorescein angiography showed late leakage in the temporal periphery, which is consistent with serous retinal detachment.
The patient had rare anterior chamber cells and 1+ vitreous cells, which is consistent with uveitis.
The optical coherence tomography revealed a posterior vitreous detachment, which is consistent with vitreous detachment.
The patient had choroidal detachments in the nasal and temporal periphery, which is consistent with choroidal detachment.
The patient had a mild nuclear sclerotic cataract in the right eye, which is consistent with cataract.
The patient had visual acuity of 20/80 in the left eye and no retinal breaks were identified, which is consistent with retinal disease.
The patient had rare anterior chamber cells and 1+ vitreous cells, which is consistent with ocular inflammation.

rationales.F01: Painful vision loss and floaters are common symptoms of posterior scleritis and serous retinal detachment.
rationales.F06: The presence of choroidal detachments, retinal detachment, and vitreous cells is highly suggestive of posterior scleritis and serous retinal detachment.
rationales.F09: Mild posterior scleral enhancement on MRI is consistent with posterior scleritis.
rationales.F12: Shallow subretinal fluid and posterior vitreous detachment on optical coherence tomography are characteristic of serous retinal detachment and vitreous detachment.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient presented with painful vision loss, floaters, and a retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid, which is consistent with serous retinal detachment, and was treated with oral prednisone for presumed serous retinal detachment secondary to posterior scleritis.
